meaning.text: Machal compares the name with the Russian word for 'forest, wood'.
Ralston states that the name Leshy or Lyeshy is derived from lyes, a forest.
Afanasyev states that the word лѣшій, in regional dialects and in old documents, means 'of the forest, wooded'.
In some places he is called Zuibochnik, from zuibka, a cradle, because he rocks himself among the branches as if in a cradle.

appearance_forms.label: Ralston's tale: young moujik with grey hair
Ordinary traveller or a friend's likeness

appearance.text: His stature depends on the height of what he inhabits: in the forests he may reach the size of high trees, in the fields he is no taller than grass.
He can alter his stature at will, at one time taller than the trees of the forest, at another shorter than the grass of the field.
He never has any eyebrows or eyelashes.
In human guise he is an old man.
He has long hair and a beard.
He has flashing green eyes.
His body is covered by a thick coat of hair.
He often appears as a peasant dressed in a sheepskin.
The sheepskin is worn ungirdled.
The left skirt of his garment is crossed over the right.
Sometimes, like a Cyclops, he has but one eye.
In his own shape he appears without clothes.
Horns spring from his forehead.
His feet are like those of a goat.
His head and body are covered with shaggy hair.
His hair is sometimes as green as that of the Rusalkas.
His fingers are tipped with long claws.
In one tale he appears as a moujik sitting on a log plaiting a bast shoe.
In that tale he looks young, but his hair is as grey as a badger's.
In the woods he frequently appears to travellers as an ordinary person or as one of their friends.
He would sometimes take the form of a traveller and engage a passer-by in conversation.
At times he takes the shape of a bear.
At times he takes the shape of a wolf.
At times he takes the shape of a hare.
He would sometimes assume the likeness of a tree by which the neighbours were accustomed to steer.

scene.text: Deep woods and fields; forests, fields and meadows are the realm he rules.
When he walks through the forest to look after his property, a rustling of the trees accompanies him.
When he goes round to inspect his domains, the forest roars around him and the trees shake.
His laughter, the peasants say, may be heard for versts around.
By night a forest-keeper might hear the wailing of a child, or groans as of someone dying; if he followed them he would probably fall into a foaming stream where none had been seen before.

variants.label: Two classes in the Governments of Kief and Chernigof (Ralston)

appearance.text: Those of the woods are giants of an ashy hue.
Those of the cornfields are, before the harvest, the same height as the growing corn.
After the harvest those of the cornfields dwindle until they are no higher than the stubble.

behavior_habitat.text: The peasants there divide the Lyeshies into two classes, one belonging to the woods and one to the cornfields.
Usually there is only one Lésiy in each wood; if there are several, a 'silvan czar' is their lord.
Some remain alone in forest solitudes and caves, while others build spacious dwellings in the woods and live there with wives and children.
The Lisunki, or forest girls and women, are female Lyeshies, hairy and hideous.
His principal business is to guard the forest.
He does not allow people to whistle or shout in the forest.
He drives away thieves, frightening them by his cries and playing pranks on them.
All the birds and beasts of the forest are under his protection.
His favourite is the bear, his only servant, who watches over him when he has drunk too much and guards him from the water-sprites.
In Little-Russia he is supposed to be the protector of the wolves.
He rocks upon the boughs, whistles, laughs and claps his hands.
He neighs like a horse, lows like a cow, barks like a dog and mews like a cat.
The echo is his work.
A strong wind constantly blows around him, so that no man has ever seen his footsteps in sand or snow.
Wherever he goes he tries to leave no track, covering his footprints with sand, leaves or snow.
He misleads those who have lost their way, removes boundary-stones and signposts, and lures wanderers into thickets and morasses.
Having led a victim into a swamp or ravine, he laughs loudly and grins at him from a little distance.
The sounds taken for echoes are said to be calls meant to lure a sportsman or woodcutter onto dangerous ground, to tickle him to death.
He blows dust into travellers' eyes and their caps off their heads, and freezes their sledges to the ground.
He entices girls and children into his copses and keeps them a long time.
Sometimes Lyeshies carry off mortal maidens and make them their wives.
In one tale a priest's daughter who strolled into the forest without leave was carried off by a Leshy and lived three years in his hut.
He substitutes his own offspring for human children; the changeling is ugly, stupid and voracious, but strong as a horse.
He brings illness on people; one who falls ill after returning from the woods is said to have crossed the Lyeshy's track.
One of his tricks is to suck the milk from cows.
Wood-demons quarrel among themselves, fighting with huge trees and rocks; the peasants say the devastation usually laid to hurricanes is their work.
By night he sleeps in a hut deep in the woods, and strives to turn out a traveller who has taken it, sweeping over it as a whirlwind.
Peasants explain the migrations of squirrels and field-mice by saying the Lyeshies are driving their flocks from one forest to another.
In 1843 peasants said migrating squirrels were the stake a Lyeshy of the Vyatka Government had gambled away to one in Vologda.
Lyeshy weddings are attended by noisy revels and violent storms, damaging cottages and felling trees on their way.
In the Government of Archangel a whirlwind is set down to a Lyeshy dancing wildly with his bride.
Usually, with the first frosts, at the start of October, the лѣшіе fall through the earth and disappear for the winter, springing out again in spring.
On leaving the forest in autumn they rage, break trees like brittle canes and drive the beasts into their burrows, while a terrible wind howls all that day.

dealing_with_it.text: A man who falls ill in the forest wraps a slice of salted bread in linen and lays it in the woods as a present for the spirit.
To be cured, the sick man carries bread and salt wrapped in a clean rag to the forest, prays over it and leaves it as a sacrifice to the Lyeshy.
Shepherds make him an offering in the shape of a cow to secure his protection for their flocks.
In the Olonetsk Government a herdsman should give the Lyeshy a cow every summer, or the spirit will destroy the whole herd.
In the Government of Archangel, if the herdsmen please him, he will see to the pasturing of the village cattle.
Huntsmen place a piece of salted bread on a tree stump and leave him the first game they take.
A sportsman offers a piece of bread or a pancake sprinkled with salt, laid on the stump of a tree.
In some districts hunters leave him the first animal they bag, in an oak forest.
The Perm peasants pray to him once a year and present him with a packet of leaf-tobacco, of which he is very fond.
A hunter's incantation calls on the 'Devils and Lyeshies' to drive the hares into his power, and the wood-demons must obey.
To avoid being led astray, one turns one's garments inside out, puts the right shoe on the left foot, or bends down to look between one's legs.
One who strikes his trail should take off his shoes and reverse their linings, and may also turn his shirt or pelisse inside out.
A forest-keeper who hears wailing or groans at night should go straight on and pay them no attention.
Neither the Lyeshy nor the Vodyany will use a pack of cards in which any clubs occur, since anything like the sign of the cross is distasteful to demons.
To invoke him, one places felled young birches in a circle with their tops in the middle, takes off one's cross, stands within and calls 'Dyedushka!' ('Grandfather!').

Or, on St. John's Eve, one fells an aspen so it falls east, stands on the stump facing east, looks between one's feet and asks 'Uncle Lyeshy' to appear just like oneself; he then appears in the form of a man.
When invoked he will bargain, giving all kinds of help in return for the invoker's soul.
A peasant will rarely sleep on a forest path for fear of a wood-demon's bridal procession crushing him.

origin.text: A popular legend says that when Satan and his hosts were expelled from heaven, some of the exiled spirits were received by the woods, which they still haunt as Lyeshie.

rationale.text: Machal records the silvan spirit Lésiy, Lésovik for the Russians, and names no source for it on these pages.
Ralston records the Lyeshy among Russian peasants of the Olonetsk and Archangel Governments and of Perm, Vyatka and Vologda, citing no other author in these passages.
Ralston records the Lyeshy as the protector of the wolves in Little-Russia, recorded here as Ukrainians; this second people rests on that single Ralston passage.
Afanasyev records the лѣшій and its regional names from Russian provinces and districts, and the belief that they vanish underground for the winter.
Ralston's tale of the Leshy in Russian Folk-Tales cites Afanasief, so it is counted with Afanasyev and not as a separate source.
Machal, Ralston and Afanasyev are three independent authors, and the verified peoples are Russians and Ukrainians, so the grade is widely-attested.

notes.text: Budget stop: of Afanasyev vol. 2 pp. 326-349 only p.326 was opened. Unread and likely relevant: afanasyev1868 pp.327-349 (the main leshy chapter: pp.329-332 shape-shifting, growth and nakedness; p.335 leshy kingdoms and the freed-captive tale; pp.336-337 drink and hunting spells; pp.340-342 leading travellers astray; pp.343, 345-346 lisunki, invocation and pacts; pp.348-349 abduction of women and weddings); afanasyev1868 pp.235, 238 (origin legend and goat-like traits); afanasyev1869 pp.311-313 (theft of unbaptised infants and changelings); afanasyev1865 p.711 (lesovik as shepherd of wolves). These would add Russian-language detail and corroboration; nothing from them is in this draft.
Ralston 1872 p.153 gives the stature-changing detail as evidence offered by 'some critics' for a storm-spirit theory; only the stated ability to alter stature is used, not the theory.

Afanasyev p.326 prints the variant as 'лису нъ (по- ли су нъ)' with OCR or line-break spacing; recorded as лисунъ and полисунъ. The page also gives a Czech equivalent, but the OCR of it is unreadable, so no Czech name or people is recorded.

Ralston's peasants of Olonetsk, Archangel, Perm, Vyatka/Vologda and Kief/Chernigof are recorded as Russians, since Ralston writes of the Russian peasant; his 'Little-Russia' is recorded as Ukrainians, by analogy with the Bohemian-to-Czechs rule. Kief and Chernigof are not tied to Little-Russia on the page.
Ralston 1872 p.373 (a spell naming 'the one-eyed Lyeshy [or wood-spirit]') was opened; it adds nothing beyond the one-eyed form on p.154 and is not cited.

verify found, not added: in the Archangel Government a Lyeshy bound by two others in a quarrel over forest rights was freed by a travelling merchant, whom he sent home in a whirlwind and helped afterwards; a traveller who will not leave the Lyeshy's hut risks being lost next day or swallowed in a swamp, at ralston1872:p.155.

verify found, not added: a Little-Russian story of a woman who covered a naked, crying baby Lyeshy with her cloak and was rewarded by its Lisunka mother with coals that turned to golden ducats; the Lyeshy is sometimes described as solitary and sometimes as having a wife and children, at ralston1872:p.159. On the second day after marriage the Lyeshy goes to the bath with his wife and they drench any passing mortal, at ralston1872:p.160.

verify found, not added: Machal says the deer and birds enjoy the silvan spirits' protection and they feast and revel with the bear, at machal1918:p.261; that the Lésiy cracks his whip, and that the recitation of certain formulae secures his services, at machal1918:p.262.
Editorial: modern video-game and fantasy depictions of the leshy (such as the antlered, skull-faced 'leshen' of the Witcher games) are excluded; this entry records only the cited folk sources.
